brief:
Review explanation

Finding the Best Split: Move a Cutoff, Compare Gini and Entropy

interactive
How does a decision tree choose where to split? Let me move a cutoff through a few labeled points, switch between Gini and entropy, and reveal the best split so I can compare it with mine.

Presentation
Static
Steps
Over time
Experiment

You will see about a dozen colored points in two classes lined up along one feature axis, a vertical cutoff line you can slide, and bars showing how mixed the left and right groups are, with the weighted impurity and the gain written out as an equation. As you move the cutoff, the counts on each side change, and so do the impurity bars and the gain. A curve of gain against every possible cutoff traces along with it, showing that the tree picks the cutoff where the weighted impurity of the two groups is lowest. The cutoff slider lets you look for the best split yourself, and the measure choice switches between Gini and entropy so you can see whether the best place stays the same. Pressing the reveal button marks the best cutoff and its score next to yours so you can compare.

ASSUMPTIONS 2
LIMITATIONS 2

findings.message: The Entropy option was not sampled, so I couldn't check the entropy readouts or the 'max 1' bar scale from the pixels. The source formula, -Σ p log2 p, is correct.

At cutoff 0, the orange gain marker sits at the origin of the gain chart and partly covers the '0' label on the y-axis. Moving the axis label further left, or clipping the marker inside the plot, would fix this.

manifest.title: Finding the Best Split: Move a Cutoff, Compare Gini and Entropy
manifest.summary: Twelve points of two classes lie on one feature axis. Slide a cutoff to split them into left and right groups. Bars show how mixed each group is, an equation gives the weighted impurity and the gain, and a curve shows the gain for every cutoff. Switch between Gini and entropy, then reveal the best split to compare it with yours.
assumptions: One feature, two classes and a fixed set of 12 points.
Points with x below the cutoff go left; the best split is searched over the midpoints between neighbouring points, as most decision trees do.
Gain is the parent impurity minus the size-weighted impurity of the two groups.
manifest.description: A horizontal axis from 0 to 10 holds 12 circles labelled A or B. A vertical line marks your cutoff. Below on the left, two bars show the impurity of the left and right groups with their class counts. On the right, a curve plots gain against cutoff, with a dot at your cutoff. An equation underneath computes the gain. After you press reveal, a green line and dot mark the best cutoff and its gain, and a message says how far your gain is from the best.
